title: 2.4 COAL
summary: Coal occupies a distinctive niche among energy commodities: it's cheap, abundant, and easy to store, but its low value relative to weight makes transportation cost the dominant factor in pricing, which in turn confines most trading to short distances and produces a thinly traded, low-volatility market compared to other fuels. The chapter traces coal from its physical and geological origins — the four ranks (lignite, sub-bituminous, bituminous, anthracite) distinguished by carbon content, and the sulfur chemistry and washing processes tied to acid rain concerns — through extraction methods (surface and underground mining) and the major producing regions (Wyoming, Appalachia) and global reserve geography. It then connects these physical realities to market structure and economics: how coal's transport constraints shape supplier relationships and pricing terminology, how the drive for generation-scale economies reshaped the electrical grid (including the AC/DC transmission history), and why coal and electricity prices remain weakly correlated despite coal's dominant role as generation fuel. A closing thread ties coal's abundance in certain nations to a broader energy-independence-versus-pollution tradeoff.
